o: It deletes Object.prototype so lookups always throw TypeError
It sets properties on a shared prototype other objects inherit
It freezes every plain object so new keys cannot be added
It copies one object's own keys onto every other object by value
questions.x: With controlled input, an attacker writes keys onto a prototype that other objects also use as a fallback. Those objects then see the new properties even though they never defined them. Object.prototype is the usual high-impact target because most plain objects inherit from it.
questions.h: Pollution does not copy keys onto every object by value. Where does it write, so later lookups on other objects see the new key?

questions.q: How does a __proto__ JSON payload pollute Object.prototype during a merge?
o: JSON.parse itself writes __proto__ keys onto Object.prototype
An unsafe merge follows __proto__ and assigns keys on that object
The V8 garbage collector copies those keys onto every heap object
A custom JSON.parse reviver replaces Object with the payload
questions.x: Payloads like {"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}} or ?__proto__[isAdmin]=true are common. JSON.parse alone does not turn that into Object.prototype pollution. A recursive merge or parser that treats __proto__ as a real path does.
questions.h: The dangerous step is not parsing JSON. It is following the __proto__ key while copying attacker fields onto nested objects.

questions.q: What does assigning through constructor.prototype pollute?
o: Only that one instance whose constructor field was overwritten
That class prototype, so later instances of the same class inherit
JSON.parse's hidden prototype and no other object in the process
The window object in every browser tab on the same machine
questions.x: Every object has a constructor pointing at the function that created it. Writing constructor.prototype.isAdmin is like User.prototype.isAdmin = true, so later User instances inherit it. A plain {} on a different chain is unaffected. A payload of {"constructor":{"prototype":{"isAdmin":true}}} aims at that path during a merge.
questions.h: constructor.prototype is that function's prototype, not automatically Object.prototype. Who inherits the new key after that write?

questions.q: What is a prototype pollution gadget?
o: A browser extension that builds __proto__ JSON payloads for you
Existing code that unsafely uses a property pollution can inject
A Node test helper that walks and prints the full prototype chain
A Proxy trap that blocks every read coming from Object.prototype
questions.x: A gadget is legitimate application code that reads a property from an ordinary object and uses it unsafely. Pollution only supplies the unexpected property. The existing code then turns that value into a logic bug or worse.
questions.h: The attacker does not upload new JavaScript. What kind of code already in the app would make an unexpected inherited property dangerous?

questions.q: Consider these claims about prototype pollution. (1) It only works in browsers, never on Node.js. (2) Only Object.prototype can ever be a useful target. (3) Gadgets require the attacker to upload a new .js file. Which option is correct?
o: None of these statements are true
Only the first claim is true
Only the first two claims are true
Only the third claim is true
questions.x: Pollution works client-side and on JavaScript backends such as Node.js. Object.prototype is the usual target, but any prototype on a trusted chain can be enough. Gadgets are already-present code paths, not attacker-uploaded scripts.
questions.h: Which of those three claims matches how merge pollution and gadgets actually work?
